action: Formulated C2 with jointly chosen seed scale and endpoint loss, proved C2 implies C1, and checked how a finite preamble changes central intervals and surplus.
output: C2 remains unproved. An elementary two-interval union shows that central-prefix coverage and its sufficient surplus bound survive adding a finite preamble. Consequently proving C1 or C2 for every uniform positive cutoff with no finite deletions is equivalent to its all-finite-deletions version. This does not assert that arbitrary deletion preserves completeness. The seed and all-future inequality remain open.

action: Test the abstract neighbouring seed principle G by an explicit infinite translated-power construction, with bounded label multiplicity and no computation process.
output: The proposed counterexample uses q minus one copies of q to the j plus one, for even q at least four and every positive cutoff k. It has divergent surplus at all prefixes, gcd one in every tail, complete modular subset sums, divergent squared irrational distances, and raw label exponent greater than one, yet its subset sums are exactly q to the k times t plus the base-q digit sum of t and have upper density at most q to the minus k. This refutes the abstract G principle only; its translated powers and duplicate supply are outside the original hypotheses. C1 and C2 remain unproved. The proof awaits independent review.

action: Track a central interval together with its all-future surplus bound and test two proposed base-initialization repairs: full modular coverage of every tail, then irrational nonconcentration and excessive raw label growth.
output: The append step preserves the tracked state and increases the covered interval strictly. The independently reviewed translated-power example makes both proposed universal abstract base-initialization assertions false at every scale, even if finitely many allowed labels are reserved as a repair supply. The strategy fails only as an abstract growth-and-arithmetic seed method. It neither refutes nor abandons C1, C2, the pure-power root, or their route. A successor must retain additional self-similar pure-power structure and prove an integer-lifting step.
